# FlexiTac Developer Handbook: full text

> FlexiTac is an open-source, full-stack platform for tactile robotics: flexible, low-cost tactile sensors (FPC-based, 32 x 12 taxels per pad), their reading boards and firmware, Python tools, real-robot data collection and robot learning with touch, and tactile simulation in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.

Every page of https://flexitac.github.io/doc/ as Markdown, in sidebar order (the reference pages last). The page index is https://flexitac.github.io/llms.txt.

# Build with FlexiTac

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/

> An open-source platform for tactile robotics, from flexible sensor design to robot learning.

Build your first sensor, customize it for your robot, and bring touch into your learning pipeline.

[Quickstart](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/) [Explore FlexiTac](https://flexitac.github.io/)

1. [Design](https://flexitac.github.io/flexitac-gen/)
   ![Render of FlexiTac sensors on both soft fingers of an xArm gripper, with one finger's sensor layers peeled apart](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/flexitac-xarm.webp)
   **FlexiTac on xArm**
   Design a sensor that fits your own robot.
   [Open FlexiTac-Gen](https://flexitac.github.io/flexitac-gen/)
2. [Build](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/)
   ![Exploded view of a FlexiTac-V2 sensor: two laminating sheets, the top FPC, the black Velostat film and the bottom FPC](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/flexitac-exploded-card.webp)
   **Build a sensor**
   Two flexible PCBs around a pressure-sensitive film. Under 3 minutes and about $4 in materials.
   [Start building](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/)
3. [Integrate](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/data-collection/)
   ![A FlexiTac sensor on the moving jaw of an SO-101 arm](https://flexitac.github.io/static/images/lerobot.jpg)
   *Teleoperation*
   ![The Touch in the Wild handheld gripper with a FlexiTac sensor on each soft finger](https://flexitac.github.io/static/images/umi.jpg)
   *UMI data*
   **Mount it and collect data**
   Teleoperate a robot with LeFlexiTac, or collect UMI data by hand with Touch in the Wild.
   [Data collection](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/data-collection/)
4. [Learn](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/imitation-learning/)
   **Learn with touch**
   Collect tactile data and train policies, on real robots or in simulation.
   - [Data collection](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/data-collection/)
   - [Representation](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/tactile-representation/)
   - [Imitation learning](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/imitation-learning/)
   - [VLA](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/vla/)
   - [Reinforcement learning](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/reinforcement-learning/)
   - [Pretraining](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/pretraining/)
   - [World models](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/world-models/)
   [Start learning](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/imitation-learning/)

# Quickstart

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/

> The whole path from ordering parts to a live tactile heatmap, with time, cost and the commands you'll run.

This guide walks you through building one **FlexiTac-V2** sensor (32 × 12 taxels), connecting it to a **32 × 16 reading board**, and streaming it live to a heatmap on your computer. This is the standard setup: the fabrication guide, the firmware and PyFlexiTac all default to it. Each step links to a detailed page.

![A FlexiTac sensor on an orange UMI soft gripper finger standing upright. Its two tails reach out to the left and end in two small FFC extenders side by side; two white flat cables with blue ends hang straight down from them, bend onto the table and run to the green 32 x 16 reading board, where an Arduino Nano sits in two sockets.](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/build-setup.webp)

*(a) The whole setup*

1. FlexiTac sensor
2. Gripper finger ([UMI](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/data-collection/#umi))
3. FFC extenders
4. Flat flexible cables
5. 32 × 16 reading board
6. Arduino Nano

![The assembled sensor pad seen from above: on the left the 24 by 64 mm sensing area with the top FPC's 12 column electrodes showing through its back; the bottom FPC's A-shaped tail runs right to its 32 gold fingers, and the top FPC's straight tail runs along the bottom, with brown stiffeners.](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/build-pad.webp)

*(b) The sensor pad, from above*

1. Sensing area
2. 32 gold fingers
3. 12 gold fingers
4. Stiffeners

> **Need a different shape or size?**
>
> Generate the two FPCs for your own gripper or fingertip with [FlexiTac-Gen](https://flexitac.github.io/flexitac-gen/). It also tells you which reading board fits your design. Ordering and fabrication work the same way. Flash and read it with your sensor's rows and columns, as described in [Match the reader to the firmware](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/pyflexitac/#rows). Designs that need the 32 × 32 board aren't covered by these docs yet.

## At a glance

**< 3 min** to fabricate one sensor

**~$4** materials per sensor

**~$30** reading board + Arduino Nano

**1–2 weeks** FPC / PCB lead time

Costs are the estimates from the [Hardware Fabrication Guide](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bvz6AL7BUkhj4Dj7n9DFXTjnGIX4-ziN8-smiCKpVZU/edit?usp=sharing) (March 2026). Cables, connectors and consumables add roughly $10.

### What you need

- **A computer** running Linux or macOS (the platforms the existing guides document), with **Python 3.11 or newer**.
- **An Arduino Nano** and a USB cable that carries data, not just power.
- **Two FPCs and one reading board**, ordered from a PCB manufacturer using the open design files (step 1).
- **Consumables:** pressure-sensitive conductive film (Velostat or Linqstat), adhesive laminating sheets and polyimide tape.
- **Flat flexible cables** (16-pin and 32-pin) and **FFC extenders** (20-pin and 40-pin) to connect the sensor to the board.

No soldering is needed to fabricate the sensor itself. You can have the reading board assembled by the manufacturer (PCBA) when you order it.

## Steps

1. **Order the parts**
   Upload the Gerber files for the top FPC, the bottom FPC and the reading board to a PCB manufacturer, and order the consumables from the bill of materials. Order a few spare sensors: they're cheap, and spares make debugging easier.
   [Bill of materials and ordering settings →](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/order-parts/)
2. **Fabricate the sensor**
   Laminate each FPC onto an adhesive sheet, put Velostat between them, seal the edges with polyimide tape and plug the gold fingers into the connectors. This takes under three minutes.
   [Step-by-step fabrication with photos →](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/fabricate/)
3. **Stream the sensor**
   Open PyFlexiTac's firmware sketch in the Arduino IDE and upload it to the reading board's Arduino Nano. Then install PyFlexiTac, find the serial port and open a live heatmap:
   ```bash
   pip install "flexitac[examples]"
   flexitac-find-port
   flexitac-heatmap --port /dev/ttyUSB0
   ```
   [Stream the sensor →](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/stream/)

## Already have an assembled sensor?

If someone handed you a working sensor and reading board, these four commands are the entire setup:

*Terminal*

```bash
pip install "flexitac[examples]"      # Python 3.11+
flexitac-flash                        # needs arduino-cli; or use the Arduino IDE
flexitac-find-port                    # which /dev/tty* is the sensor
flexitac-heatmap --port /dev/ttyUSB0  # press the pad
```

## You're done when…

- `flexitac-stream` ([Check the signal](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/pyflexitac/#stream)) reports a steady frame rate (about **100+ fps** for a 32 × 12 sensor).
- `raw_max` changes when you press the sensor, and isn't stuck at 0 or 255.
- A bright spot in `flexitac-heatmap` follows your fingertip across **every** row and column.

> **Stuck?**
>
> Most first-time problems are a serial permission, a cable that only charges, or firmware and reader disagreeing on the number of rows. [Troubleshooting](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/troubleshooting/) covers each of these by symptom. You can also ask on the [Discord](https://discord.gg/6gw887Vxms).


---

# Order parts

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/order-parts/

> Design files, the bill of materials, and the manufacturer settings for the FPCs and the reading board.

You need three things for a FlexiTac-V2 setup: the **two sensor FPCs** and the **reading board** from a PCB manufacturer, plus a few **off-the-shelf parts** (Arduino Nano, cables, consumables). Fabrication takes 1–2 weeks including shipping, so order everything at once.

> **Source of truth**
>
> This page summarizes the [FlexiTac Hardware Fabrication Guide](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bvz6AL7BUkhj4Dj7n9DFXTjnGIX4-ziN8-smiCKpVZU/edit?usp=sharing) (March 2026). If anything here disagrees with the guide, follow the guide, and please [report it](https://github.com/FlexiTac/FlexiTac.github.io/issues/new?title=Docs:+Order+parts&labels=documentation) so we can fix this page.

## Design files

| Part | Files | Download |
|---|---|---|
| **Top FPC** (V2 sensor) | Gerber, EasyEDA Pro export of 2026-03-02 | [Gerber_Top_FPC_2026-03-02.zip](https://flexitac.github.io/flexitac-gen/static/vendor/flexitac-v2/Gerber_Top_FPC_2026-03-02.zip) |
| **Bottom FPC** (V2 sensor) | Gerber, EasyEDA Pro export of 2026-03-02 | [Gerber_Bottom_FPC_2026-03-02.zip](https://flexitac.github.io/flexitac-gen/static/vendor/flexitac-v2/Gerber_Bottom_FPC_2026-03-02.zip) |
| **Reading board 32 × 16** (recommended) | Gerber, BOM, pick-and-place | [FlexiTac_reading_board_32x16.zip](https://flexitac.github.io/flexitac-gen/static/vendor/flexitac-reader/FlexiTac_reading_board_32x16.zip) · [schematic (PDF)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1KEzet6f4s1i1d-GOSpwD5-4Peu2S67hL/view?usp=drive_link) |
| **Reading board 32 × 32** (development) | Gerber, BOM, pick-and-place | [FlexiTac_reading_board_32x32.zip](https://flexitac.github.io/flexitac-gen/static/vendor/flexitac-reader/FlexiTac_reading_board_32x32.zip) · [schematic (PDF)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bmmO034ZeR81Ba8OML_0MlkXvKADsflr/view?usp=drive_link) |

The downloads are unchanged copies of the files linked from the guide's "PCB Related Files" table, served from FlexiTac-Gen. Each reading-board ZIP bundles that board's Gerber ZIP, BOM and pick-and-place file; unzip it and upload the inner `Gerber_*.zip` as the Gerber.

[![Top FPC layout of the FlexiTac-V2 sensor: 12 column electrodes with slots between them, and a tail to the gold fingers](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/v2-fpc-top.svg)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/v2-fpc-top.svg)

*Top FPC*

[![Bottom FPC layout of the FlexiTac-V2 sensor: 32 row electrodes with slots between them, and an A-shaped tail to the gold fingers](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/v2-fpc-bottom.svg)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/v2-fpc-bottom.svg)

*Bottom FPC*

### Which reading board?

Order the **32 × 16 board**. According to the Fabrication Guide, this board is enough to read the V2 sensor, and the firmware and PyFlexiTac support it out of the box.

[![FlexiTac 32 × 16 reading board with an Arduino Nano and two FFC connectors](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/reading-board-32x16-cut.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/reading-board-32x16-cut.webp)

*32 × 16 reading board (use this one)*

[![FlexiTac 32 × 32 reading board](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/reading-board-32x32-cut.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/reading-board-32x32-cut.webp)

*32 × 32 reading board (development)*

| Board | Reads | Connectors | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **32 × 16** | Up to 32 lines on one side and 16 on the other | 32-pin + 16-pin FFC | FlexiTac-V2, and custom sensors that fit within 32 × 16 |
| **32 × 32** | Up to 32 lines on each side | 32-pin + 32-pin FFC | Larger custom sensors and development. Its firmware isn't covered by these docs yet. |

If you designed a custom sensor with [FlexiTac-Gen](https://flexitac.github.io/flexitac-gen/), the app tells you which board fits it.

> **Order spares**
>
> FPCs are cheap at quantity: about **$2.57 per top + bottom pair at 100 units**. Order a few extra sensors. Spares let you swap out a damaged sensor in seconds and tell a bad sensor from a bad board.

## Bill of materials

Prices and links are the ones in the Fabrication Guide. A quantity like 0.05 means one roll or sheet covers about 20 sensors.

### Sensor: about $4 each

| # | Part | Qty per sensor | Price | Where |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Top and bottom FPC** (key component) | 1 pair | $2.5 | PCB manufacturer, [see below](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/order-parts/#order-the-fpcs) |
| 2 | Polyimide tape (4 in × 108 ft) | 0.01 | $21.98 | [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07N4QTXWS) |
| 3 | Pressure-sensitive conductive sheet (Velostat / Linqstat) | 0.05 | $4.95 | [Adafruit 1361](https://www.adafruit.com/product/1361) |
| 4 | Adhesive laminating sheets | 0.01 | $6.29 | [Amazon](https://a.co/d/02y7MDdy) |

### Reading board: about $30

| # | Part | Qty | Price | Where |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | **Reading board PCB** (key component) | 1 | $5 | PCB manufacturer, [see below](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/order-parts/#order-the-reading-board) |
| 6 | Arduino Nano | 1 | $25.10 | [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0097AU5OU) |

### Cables and connectors: about $10

| # | Part | Qty | Price | Where |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | Flexible flat cable, 32-pin | 1 | $5.09 (5-pack) | [Amazon](https://a.co/d/0aJnyShh) |
| 8 | Flexible flat cable, 16-pin | 1 | $6.09 (5-pack) | [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07RWF5D83) |
| 9 | Mini-USB cable (must carry data) | 1 | $11.99 (2-pack) | [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B091SQKMQK) |
| 10 | 20-pin FFC extender | 1 | $0.95 | [Adafruit 5203](https://www.adafruit.com/product/5203) |
| 11 | 40-pin FFC extender | 1 | $0.95 | [Adafruit 4523](https://www.adafruit.com/product/4523) |
| 12 | FFC extender, easy-install alternative to #10–11 | 2 | $0.55–0.88 | [AliExpress](https://www.aliexpress.us/item/3256801662408481.html) |

> **Which FFC extenders?**
>
> The Adafruit extenders (#10, #11) used in the video are compact but need careful alignment and some practice to install. The AliExpress extenders (#12) are easier to install, although bulkier. On AliExpress, select the **16-pin** and **32-pin** variants.

## Order the FPCs

The guide's screenshots use JLCPCB's online quote. Order the top and bottom FPCs as two separate designs.

1. **Upload the Gerber and choose Flex**
   Upload `Gerber_Top_FPC_2026-03-02.zip`. Set **Base Material** to **Flex**, keep 2 layers and choose your quantity.
   [![PCB quote form with Flex selected as the base material](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/order-fpc-flex.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/order-fpc-flex.webp)
   *Base material: Flex, 2 layers.*
2. **Set the thickness to 0.2 mm**
   Under **PCB Specifications**, set **PCB Thickness** to **0.2 mm**. You can leave the other options at their defaults, as in the screenshot (yellow coverlay, ENIG finish).
   [![PCB specifications with 0.2 mm thickness selected](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/order-fpc-specs.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/order-fpc-specs.webp)
   *PCB Thickness: 0.2 mm.*
3. **Enable gold fingers**
   Under **High-spec Options**, set **Gold Fingers: Yes** and **Gold Fingers Thickness: 0.3 mm**. The gold fingers are the ends that plug into the FFC connectors. The V2 Gerbers include a stiffener layer under them, which the quote form picks up automatically ("Based on EasyEDA Stiffener Layer").
   [![High-spec options with Gold Fingers set to Yes and thickness 0.3 mm highlighted](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/order-fpc-goldfinger.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/order-fpc-goldfinger.webp)
   *Gold Fingers: Yes, thickness 0.3 mm.*
4. **Repeat for the bottom FPC**
   Repeat steps 1–3 with `Gerber_Bottom_FPC_2026-03-02.zip`. The bottom FPC needs the same thickness and gold fingers. At a 100-unit scale, a top + bottom pair costs about $2.57.

## Order the reading board

Have the manufacturer assemble the board (PCBA) so the components arrive already soldered.

1. **Upload the Gerber and enable assembly**
   Upload the reading board's Gerber (`Gerber_16_32.zip` for the 32 × 16 board). Keep **FR-4**, 2 layers, then enable **PCB Assembly** with the assembly side set as in the guide (**Bottom**).
   [![Quote form for the 32 × 16 reading board on FR-4](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/order-pcba.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/order-pcba.webp)
   *The 32 × 16 reading board in the quote form.*
2. **Upload the BOM and pick-and-place files**
   Upload `BOM_05mm_FFC_16_32_1mux_4sr_2025-11-01.csv` and `PickAndPlace_PCB_05mm_FFC_16_32_1mux_4sr_2025-11-01.csv`. Check that every component is in stock. If a part is out of stock, choose an equivalent before you continue.
   [![BOM and pick-and-place upload fields](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/order-pcba-bom.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/order-pcba-bom.webp)
   *Upload the BOM and the pick-and-place (CPL) file.*
3. **Review the placement**
   Check the assembly draft and the 3D render: every part should sit on its footprint and face the right way.
   [![3D render of the assembled reading board](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/order-pcba-review.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/order-pcba-review.webp)
   *Review the 3D render before you order.*
4. **Place the order**
   The quoted price covers 5 boards. Delivery takes about one week.

# Fabricate a sensor

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/fabricate/

> Turn two FPCs, a piece of Velostat and some tape into a working FlexiTac-V2 sensor in under three minutes.

Fabricating a FlexiTac-V2 sensor is mostly lamination: no soldering, and no special tools beyond scissors or a craft knife. Once you have done it once, a sensor takes under three minutes.

> **Watch it first**
>
> The steps below follow the [fabrication video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HYmMbsrwWFA). It's worth watching once before your first build.

## Materials

[![Workspace with the two FPCs, lamination sheets, Velostat and a roll of polyimide tape](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-materials.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-materials.webp)

*Everything for one sensor: the top and bottom FPCs, adhesive lamination sheets, Velostat and polyimide tape.*

| Item | BOM # | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Top FPC and bottom FPC | 1 | One of each per sensor |
| Adhesive laminating sheets | 4 | Two pre-cut pieces, one per FPC |
| Velostat / Linqstat | 3 | One piece that covers the electrode area |
| Polyimide tape | 2 | For sealing the edges |
| FFC extenders (16- and 32-pin) and flat cables | 7–12 | For connecting to the reading board in step 4 |
| Assembled reading board | 5–6 | Flashed or not; you can flash it later |

See [Order parts](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/order-parts/#bom) for the full bill of materials.

## How the layers stack

A FlexiTac sensor is five thin layers. Both FPCs turn their copper electrodes toward the Velostat in the middle: the top FPC's 12 columns face down and the bottom FPC's 32 rows face up. Wherever a row crosses a column there is a taxel, and pressing it squeezes the film between the two electrodes.

![Exploded view of a FlexiTac-V2 sensor. From top to bottom: a clear laminating sheet, the top FPC seen from its back with 12 column electrodes, the black Velostat film, the bottom FPC with 32 row electrodes facing up, and a second laminating sheet. Both FPC tails run out to the same side.](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/flexitac-exploded.webp)

1. **Laminating sheet** holds the top FPC from behind.
2. **Top FPC**: 12 column electrodes, copper side down. You see its back here, with the copper showing through.
3. **Velostat**: the pressure-sensitive film, cut to cover the electrode area.
4. **Bottom FPC**: 32 row electrodes, copper side up.
5. **Laminating sheet** holds the bottom FPC from behind.

Steps 1 and 2 below build exactly this stack: each FPC on its own laminating sheet, then the Velostat between them. Both tails leave on the same side. Step 3 then seals the edges with polyimide tape.

## Build the sensor

1. **Attach each FPC to a lamination sheet and align it**
   Peel a pre-cut lamination sheet and attach the **top FPC** to it. Do the same with the **bottom FPC** on a second sheet. Align the corners exactly, as in the photos: the two layers must line up when you stack them in step 2.
   [![Peeling the backing from a lamination sheet](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step1-laminate.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step1-laminate.webp)
   *Peel the lamination sheet.*
   [![Placing the FPC onto the adhesive sheet](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step1-align.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step1-align.webp)
   *Place the FPC, corners aligned.*
   [![An FPC laminated onto its sheet, held up to the camera](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step1-laminated.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step1-laminated.webp)
   *One laminated FPC layer.*
2. **Stack the Velostat between the two layers**
   Place the Velostat in the middle, between the two prepared layers, centered over the electrode area. Close the stack with the second layer. **Once it's centered, the sensor stack already works.**
   [![Placing a black Velostat sheet over a laminated FPC](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step2-velostat.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step2-velostat.webp)
   *Center the Velostat over the electrodes.*
   [![Closing the sensor stack with the second FPC layer](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step2-close.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step2-close.webp)
   *Close the stack with the other layer.*
3. **Seal the edges with polyimide tape**
   Lay out a strip of polyimide tape and seal the border of the stack. This doesn't change how the sensor works. It holds the layers in place and keeps the sensor intact through long experiments.
   [![Placing the sensor stack on a strip of polyimide tape](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step3-polyimide.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step3-polyimide.webp)
   *Place the stack on the tape.*
   [![Folding the polyimide tape around the sensor edges](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step3-sealed.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step3-sealed.webp)
   *Fold the tape around the edges.*
4. **Connect to the reading board**
   Insert each sensor's **gold fingers** into an FFC connector (extender), then run a flat flexible cable from each connector to the reading board. The wider gold-finger end takes the 40-pin extender (or the 32-pin AliExpress one) and the 32-pin cable. The narrower one takes the 20-pin extender (or the 16-pin one) and the 16-pin cable.
   [![The sealed sensor with the reading board, two flat flexible cables and FFC connectors](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step4-parts.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step4-parts.webp)
   *Sealed sensor, reading board, flat cables and connectors.*
   [![Inserting the FPC gold fingers into a connector](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step4-insert.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step4-insert.webp)
   *Insert the gold fingers into the connector.*
   [![Attaching a flat flexible cable to the connector](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step4-cable.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step4-cable.webp)
   *Attach the flat cable.*
   [![Finished sensor connected through two flat cables to the reading board](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step4-connected.webp)](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/fab-step4-connected.webp)
   *Done: the sensor is connected to the reading board.*

## Tips for a good sensor

- **Fully seat the gold fingers.** Push each FPC end all the way into its connector, straight and not skewed. The Adafruit extenders are wider than the gold fingers, so push the fingers against one side of the opening as you insert them; the side keeps them square. A finger that's half-seated, skewed or off by one pin is the most common cause of dead, swapped or [shorted rows](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/troubleshooting/#short).
- **Mind the cable orientation.** FFC contacts are on one side only. If a whole sensor reads nothing, check that each cable's contacts face the connector contacts at both ends.
- **The Adafruit extenders need practice.** They're compact but take careful alignment. The AliExpress extenders (BOM #12) are bulkier but easier to install.
- **Keep the Velostat covering every crossing.** Taxels outside the film won't respond. An off-center film shows up as a dead edge on the heatmap.
- **Make a few at once.** Sensors are consistent enough that spares are interchangeable, and having one makes it easy to tell a bad sensor from a bad board.

> **How long does a sensor last?**
>
> In the authors' experience, sensors stay consistent for about a year of use without significant degradation. Some teams have collected thousands of demonstrations without breaking one. If a sensor is damaged, replace it. Swapping in a new sensor typically doesn't noticeably affect performance.

## Next

Your sensor is wired to the reading board. Now [stream the sensor](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/stream/).


---

# Stream the sensor

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/stream/

> Flash the reading board from the Arduino IDE, then watch a live heatmap follow your finger. That's a working sensor.

The Arduino Nano on the reading board runs a small sketch that scans the sensor and streams frames over USB. Flash it once, then watch a bright spot follow your finger on a live heatmap. That's a working sensor.

## Flash the reading board

1. **Get the sketch**
   Download PyFlexiTac's [firmware sketch](https://github.com/WT-MM/PyFlexiTac/blob/master/flexitac/firmware/template.ino) (**Download raw file** on that page) and open it in the [Arduino IDE](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software). Let the IDE move it into a folder of the same name. It is already set up for the V2 sensor: 12 rows, 32 columns, 2,000,000 baud.
2. **Select the board and port**
   **Tools → Board → Arduino AVR Boards → Arduino Nano**, then pick the serial port under **Tools → Port**. If the upload fails with `not in sync`, set **Tools → Processor → ATmega328P (Old Bootloader)** and try again.
3. **Upload**
   Click **Upload**. You only need to do this once per board.

## See the first signal

1. **Install PyFlexiTac**
   Its live heatmap shows what the sensor feels. It needs **Python 3.11 or newer**.
   ```bash
   python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
   pip install "flexitac[examples]"
   ```
2. **Find the serial port**
   ```bash
   flexitac-find-port
   ```
   It asks you to unplug the board and reports the port that disappeared, such as `/dev/ttyUSB0` on Linux or `/dev/tty.usbserial-*` on macOS.
3. **Open the live heatmap**
   ```bash
   flexitac-heatmap --port /dev/ttyUSB0
   ```
   Don't touch the sensor for the first second, while it measures each taxel's resting level. Then press with a fingertip and drag it slowly across the pad.

**A bright spot that follows your finger across every row and column means your sensor works.** If a row or column never lights up, see [Dead rows or columns](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/troubleshooting/#dead-rows).

> **`Permission denied` on Linux?**
>
> Add yourself to the `dialout` group once, then log out and back in: `sudo usermod -aG dialout "$USER"`. More in [Serial port permissions](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/pyflexitac/#permissions).

## Next

**[PyFlexiTac](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/pyflexitac/)**

Read frames in your own Python code, record datasets, run several sensors, check the signal, flash from the command line, and the wire protocol.

**[Collect tactile data](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/data-collection/)**

Mount the sensor on a gripper and record demonstrations with touch, then train a policy on them.

**[Troubleshooting](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/troubleshooting/)**

No port, no frames, a scrambled picture or dead rows, by symptom.

# Troubleshooting & FAQ

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/troubleshooting/

> Find your symptom, then work through the checks from most to least likely.

Start with `flexitac-stream --port <port>`. Its output (fps, `raw_max`, `norm_max`) tells you which layer is failing:

- **Frames arrive at full rate, but some taxels are dead, stuck or light up in the wrong place:** the sensor, its connectors or its cables. See [Hardware problems](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/troubleshooting/#hardware).
- **No serial port, no frames, a failed upload, or a picture that's wrong across the whole sensor:** the reading board's firmware, the USB connection or the reader settings. See [Firmware and reading problems](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/troubleshooting/#firmware).

## Hardware problems

These stay with the sensor, a connector or a cable. If you have a spare, swapping it in moves the fault with it.

### Rows with gaps, dead rows or identical readings

*Example: Gold fingers that went into their extender at an angle. Each press lights up two patches in the same column instead of one.*

Typical signs:

- **A press lights up rows with gaps between them**, as in the video.
- **Some rows never light up.**
- **Neighboring taxels show exactly the same reading.**

The usual cause is gold fingers or a flat cable that went into an FFC extender at an angle. The extender joins each gold finger to its own wire in the cable. A crooked finger can touch two contacts, which shorts two lines into one, or miss its contact. The [20-pin extender](https://www.adafruit.com/product/5203) is wider than the sensor's 12 gold fingers and the 16-pin cable, so both can go in crooked. Push the gold fingers against one side of the opening as you slide them in; the side keeps them square.

The animation needs JavaScript. In short: push the gold fingers in straight, against one side of the connector, so each finger touches exactly one contact.

*Schematic top view of the 20-pin extender, not to scale. The skew is exaggerated for clarity.*

To fix it:

1. **Open the connector.** Gently pry up its two ears and pull the gold fingers out.
2. **Insert the gold fingers against one side** of the opening, straight and all the way in, with the contacts facing up. Then push the ears back in.
3. **Check the flat cable the same way** at the other end of the extender: straight, all the way in, contacts up, and against the same side as the fingers. It is narrower than its connector too.
4. **Test.** Run `flexitac-stream --port <port>` and press one spot at a time. Each press should light up one patch.

The 32-pin gold fingers and cable go into the [40-pin extender](https://www.adafruit.com/product/4523) the same way.

### Some rows or columns never respond

Run `flexitac-stream --port <port> --per-row` and press along a column. Then check:

- **Gold fingers fully and squarely seated** in each FFC extender, pushed against one side of the opening (see [above](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/troubleshooting/#short)). Re-seat both ends and both cables.
- **Cable orientation.** A cable inserted with its contacts facing the wrong way gives a whole dead side.
- **Velostat coverage.** A dead band along one edge often means the film doesn't reach that edge.
- **Lamination alignment.** If the top and bottom FPCs were offset when you stacked them, edge crossings may not overlap.
- **Expected dead rows:** with `32_16_fast.ino` on a V2 sensor, rows 0–3 are unconnected by design.
- **Swap parts to isolate the fault.** Try a spare sensor on the same board, then the same sensor on another board.

### `raw_max` is stuck at 0 or 255

A value that stays flat at either end of the range points to a **wiring problem**, such as a disconnected or [shorted](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/troubleshooting/#short) line, not a flashing problem. Re-seat the connectors and inspect the gold fingers and cables for damage.

### The signal saturates or barely changes

- **Saturates under light touch:** the sensor may be pre-loaded by its mount, or the baseline was captured under load. Re-calibrate at rest.
- **Barely changes under firm pressure:** check that the Velostat is present and centered, and that the polyimide seal isn't holding the layers apart. Make sure you're reading the right port, and not another device.

## Firmware and reading problems

These come from the reading board's firmware, the USB connection or how the reader is set up. The sensor itself is usually fine.

### No serial port appears

- **Try another USB cable.** Many mini-USB cables only carry power. If the Nano's LED lights up but no port appears, the cable is the most likely cause.
- **Check the USB driver.** Many Nano clones use a CH340 USB-serial chip. Recent Linux and macOS versions include a driver. On older systems, install the CH340 driver from the chip vendor.
- **Look at the kernel log** (Linux) while you plug the board in:
  ```bash
  # expect e.g. "ch341-uart converter now attached to ttyUSB0"
  sudo dmesg -w
  ```
- On Linux, **`brltty` can grab CH340 devices.** If the port appears and immediately disappears, removing that package (`sudo apt remove brltty`) is a common fix.

### Permission denied

Your user can't open the serial device. On Linux, add yourself to `dialout` and log in again:

```bash
sudo usermod -aG dialout "$USER"
```

See [Serial port permissions](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/pyflexitac/#permissions) for macOS and temporary workarounds.

### Flashing fails

| Message | Fix |
|---|---|
| `arduino-cli not found on PATH` | Install `arduino-cli` and run `arduino-cli core install arduino:avr`. See [Flash from the command line](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/pyflexitac/#flexitac-flash). |
| `no Arduino board detected` | Clones often don't report a board type. Pass `--port` and `--fqbn arduino:avr:nano`. |
| `multiple boards detected` | Unplug the other boards, or pass `--port` and `--fqbn` explicitly. |
| Upload hangs or says `not in sync` | Old-bootloader Nano: use `--fqbn arduino:avr:nano:cpu=atmega328old` (in the IDE: **Processor → ATmega328P (Old Bootloader)**). |
| `Permission denied` | See [Permission denied](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/troubleshooting/#permission-denied). Close the Arduino IDE serial monitor and any other program holding the port. |

### No frames, `fps=0` or `TimeoutError`

The port opens, but the reader never finds a start marker (`0xAA 0x55`) followed by a full frame.

1. **Re-flash.** A board fresh from the factory, or one running another sketch, isn't sending FlexiTac frames.
2. **Check the baud rate.** Both sides must use 2,000,000 unless you changed it on purpose. At the wrong rate, the bytes arrive garbled and no marker is ever found.
3. **Check the port.** Make sure you're reading the reading board and not another serial device. `flexitac-find-port` tells you which one it is.
4. **Close other programs** that might be reading the same port (serial monitor, a second script).

### The heatmap looks scrambled or shifted

Frames arrive, but the picture is wrong. This usually means a **row-count mismatch** between the firmware you flashed and the reader:

| What you see | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Normal fps, but the top 4 rows never respond and touches near one end of the sensor don't show | Firmware sends 16 rows (`32_16_fast.ino`), reader expects 12 | Read with `--rows 16`, or flash PyFlexiTac's sketch instead |
| Frame rate drops to about half, and the bottom 4 rows echo touches on the top rows | Firmware sends 12 rows, reader expects 16 | Read with the defaults (12 rows) |
| A round touch shows up as a slanted streak (each row shifted a little further sideways) | `--cols` doesn't match the firmware | Use the same `--cols` the firmware was built with (32 for V2) |

See [Match the reader to the firmware](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/pyflexitac/#rows) for which reader settings go with which firmware.

### Noisy or drifting at rest

- **Re-calibrate with nothing touching the sensor.** If the sensor was pressed during the first ~30 frames, the baseline is wrong. Call `sensor.calibrate()` or restart the stream.
- **Mounting changes the baseline.** Bending or pre-loading the sensor onto a curved finger raises its resting values. Calibrate after mounting, not before.
- **Expect small fluctuations.** `normalized` hides readings below the threshold (default 25 counts above baseline). If you work with `raw`, apply your own threshold or temporal filter. The hardware repo's `fast_32_16.py` uses an exponential filter with α = 0.2.

### Low frame rate

About 100+ fps is expected for 12 × 32 at 2 Mbaud. Lower rates usually come from a slow USB hub, a very busy host, or a visualizer that renders every frame. For live use, call `read_latest()` so rendering never falls behind.

## FAQ

### How long do FPC and PCB orders take?

Usually 1–2 weeks from order to delivery for the FPCs and PCBs, depending on your location and shipping method. An assembled reading board takes about one week.

### How durable is the sensor?

In the authors' experience, sensors stay consistent and can often be used for about a year without significant degradation. Some teams have collected thousands of demonstrations without breaking one.

### What if a sensor is damaged or malfunctioning?

Order a few spare sensors up front. Replacing a damaged sensor with a new one typically doesn't noticeably affect performance, so sensors are consistent across instances.

### Can I use FlexiTac commercially?

The hardware is licensed [CC BY-NC 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/), which doesn't cover commercial use. Software projects in the ecosystem have their own licenses; PyFlexiTac, for example, is MIT-licensed.

## Still stuck?

Ask on the [FlexiTac Discord](https://discord.gg/6gw887Vxms), or open an issue in the repository that owns the problem:

| Problem with | Open an issue in |
|---|---|
| Sensor design, reading board, `32_16_fast.ino` | [FlexiTac/FlexiTac](https://github.com/FlexiTac/FlexiTac/issues) |
| `flexitac-*` commands, the Python API, `flexitac-flash` firmware | [WT-MM/PyFlexiTac](https://github.com/WT-MM/PyFlexiTac/issues) |
| These docs | [FlexiTac/FlexiTac.github.io](https://github.com/FlexiTac/FlexiTac.github.io/issues) |

A report anyone can act on includes: sensor version or geometry, reading board (32 × 16 or 32 × 32), which firmware you flashed and its settings, OS and Python version, the exact command you ran, the full output, and a photo of the connections.

# Next steps

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/next-steps/

> Learn on a real robot or in simulation, customize the sensor, and share and cite what you build.

You have a sensor streaming data. What comes next depends on your goal. Each section below points to the page or project that owns that part of the ecosystem.

## Learn with touch

**[Collect tactile data](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/data-collection/)**

Mount the sensor and record visuo-tactile demonstrations, with LeFlexiTac on a low-cost arm or Touch in the Wild with a handheld gripper.

**[Tactile simulation](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/simulation/)**

Build the FlexiTac simulation in Isaac Sim, replay tactile trajectories and record demonstrations in the browser. Plus VT-Refine.

## Customize the sensor

**[FlexiTac-Gen](https://flexitac.github.io/flexitac-gen/)**

Generate the two FPCs of a FlexiTac sensor for your own gripper, fingertip or hand, in the browser. Pick a preset or fit to a surface of your STL part, choose the resolution, and download manufacturing files. The [source and docs](https://github.com/FlexiTac/FlexiTac/tree/main/flexitac-gen) are in the hardware repo.

**[Learn FlexiTac](https://flexitac.github.io/learn/)**

An interactive course on how a resistive tactile array senses, how it's scanned, and what the numbers mean. Useful before you change the hardware.

## Share what you build

FlexiTac grows through the people who build with it. Whatever you made, a mount, a fix or a whole robot, it helps the next person.

- **Fix or extend these docs.** Every page has an **Edit page** link. Tested a new sensor/board combination, or found a step that tripped you up? Send a pull request.
- **Add your paper or project** to [Awesome FlexiTac](https://binghao-huang.github.io/Awesome-FlexiTac/) by [opening an issue or PR](https://github.com/binghao-huang/Awesome-FlexiTac/issues) (see its [contributing guide](https://github.com/binghao-huang/Awesome-FlexiTac/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)).
- **Show your build** on the [Discord](https://discord.gg/6gw887Vxms): photos, CAD for your mount, firmware settings and what didn't work are all welcome.
- **Report bugs** in the repository that owns the code (see [Still stuck?](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/troubleshooting/#help)).
- **Star** [FlexiTac on GitHub](https://github.com/FlexiTac/FlexiTac) so others can find it.

## Cite FlexiTac

If FlexiTac helps your research, please cite:

*flexitac.bib*

```bibtex
@article{huang2026flexitac,
  title   = {FlexiTac: A Low-Cost, Open-Source, Scalable Tactile Sensing Solution for Robotic Systems},
  author  = {Huang, Binghao and Li, Yunzhu},
  journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.28156},
  year    = {2026}
}
```

If you use PyFlexiTac or LeFlexiTac, please also cite those projects. Their citations are in their READMEs.

# Data collection

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/data-collection/

> Two ways to record touch together with vision and actions, by teleoperation or with a handheld UMI gripper.

A tactile demonstration records what the sensor feels, what the camera sees and what the gripper does, all at the same moments. There are two ways to collect one.

**New to robot learning?** Start with teleoperation. It is the lowest-cost setup and uses the sensor exactly as these docs set it up.

## Teleoperation

You move a leader arm and the follower robot copies it, so the recorded actions are the robot's own. The open setup is [LeFlexiTac](https://tna001-ai.github.io/LeFlexiTac/), which adds FlexiTac to [LeRobot](https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot) on the low-cost SO-100/101 arm.

- **Robot:** SO-100/101 leader and follower arms, a camera and a Linux machine
- **Sensor:** One standard FlexiTac sensor (32 × 12), on the follower's 3D-printed moving jaw only
- **Reader:** PyFlexiTac, with the firmware from [Stream the sensor](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/stream/)
- **Output:** A LeRobot dataset: the tactile map next to the camera and joint states, at 30 fps

*Sample: Recording a LeFlexiTac demonstration. The leader arm (right) drives the follower, and the screen shows the tactile map and camera view going into the dataset.*

The full guide is **steps 01–08** of the [LeFlexiTac docs](https://tna001-ai.github.io/LeFlexiTac/docs.html#reproduction), from building the robot to collecting data. In short:

1. **Build the arm and the tactile jaw**
   Assemble the arms from the [SO-ARM100 guide](https://github.com/TheRobotStudio/SO-ARM100), then print LeFlexiTac's Moving Jaw and Wrist Roll and fit them.
2. **Install LeFlexiTac**
   Install the [fork](https://github.com/TNA001-AI/lerobot_tactile) from source in a Python 3.12 environment. `pip install lerobot` gives you upstream LeRobot, which has no tactile support.
3. **Calibrate the arms and mount the sensor**
   Calibrate and test teleoperation with [LeRobot's SO-101 walkthrough](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/il_robots), then mount the sensor and confirm it with `flexitac-heatmap`.
4. **Record demonstrations**
   Record with `lerobot-record` and the `so_tactile_follower` robot type.

Then train [ACT or Diffusion Policy](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/imitation-learning/#leflexitac), or [Pi0.5 and SmolVLA](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/vla/#leflexitac), on your dataset.

## UMI data

You hold a [UMI](https://github.com/real-stanford/universal_manipulation_interface)-style gripper and do the task yourself, indoors or outdoors, with no robot. A GoPro on the gripper records vision, and a FlexiTac sensor on each soft finger records touch. The open setup is [Touch in the Wild](https://binghao-huang.github.io/touch_in_the_wild/) (NeurIPS 2025). Its authors used it to collect more than 2,700 demonstrations across 43 tasks in 12 environments.

- **Gripper:** The UMI handheld gripper with Touch in the Wild's modifications, and a GoPro Hero 9
- **Sensors:** Two standard FlexiTac sensors (32 × 12), one on each soft finger
- **Reader:** ROS 2 Humble on Ubuntu 22.04, with older text-format firmware (see the caution below)
- **Output:** GoPro video and tactile streams, turned into a training dataset by a SLAM pipeline
- **Shared data:** The [Touch in the Wild dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/binghaohuang-robot/touch_in_the_wild-dataset). The pretraining set alone is about 88 GB.

Outdoors

Shelf

Workbench

*Sample data: Three demonstrations from Touch in the Wild: the GoPro's fish-eye view, with the left and right fingers' tactile maps below it.*

1. **Build the gripper**
   Build the UMI gripper, then apply Touch in the Wild's top plate and finger holders and add the two sensors. [Gripper guide](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Gxd2PzVo-sH_XbvnVw_r3eI5i3I3t0rr7JdhpN1PJMA/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.dcjpnwh7wh40)
2. **Set up the recording laptop**
   Give each reading board a fixed device name, then install the ROS 2 tactile packages. [Device names](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild-data-collection#udev) · [ROS 2 setup](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild-data-collection#ros)
3. **Collect demonstrations**
   Record the tactile streams with ROS 2 while the GoPro films. [Data collection protocol](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild-data-collection#protocol)
4. **Turn the recordings into a dataset**
   Run the SLAM pipeline on the session folder. [README: SLAM pipeline](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild#creating-a-dataset-with-the-slam-pipeline)

> **It needs different firmware**
>
> Touch in the Wild reads the boards with its own code, not PyFlexiTac: a ROS 2 node while recording, and serial readers when running a policy. Both expect the older **text** output, 16 lines of 32 numbers per frame. The firmware in [Stream the sensor](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/stream/#flash) sends **binary** frames instead, so a board flashed from these docs won't work with Touch in the Wild as it is, and its repositories don't include matching firmware. Ask in its [issues](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild/issues) or on the [Discord](https://discord.gg/6gw887Vxms) before you build.

Next, [pretrain the visuo-tactile encoder](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/pretraining/#touch-in-the-wild) or start from the released one, then train a [Diffusion Policy](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/imitation-learning/#touch-in-the-wild).

## Good data, either way

- **Mount on something slightly soft,** such as a fin-ray finger, so contact spreads over several taxels.
- **Keep the cable still at the connector.** Route the flat cable so it doesn't flex while the gripper moves.
- **Calibrate after mounting.** The mount itself changes the resting baseline.
- **Keep touch in sync.** LeFlexiTac records touch into the same dataset frames as the camera and joints, so train and run a policy at the frame rate you recorded at. Touch in the Wild shows a QR code to the camera before each demonstration to line up video and touch. In your own setup, record with PyFlexiTac's `sensor.read()` so no frame is skipped, and keep each frame's `timestamp_s` ([Read frames in Python](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/pyflexitac/#python)).
- **Another gripper?** [FlexiTac-Gen](https://flexitac.github.io/flexitac-gen/) designs a sensor that fits it.


---

# Tactile representation

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/tactile-representation/

> Give touch to a policy as a 2D map per pad, or as 3D tactile points in one point cloud with the camera's, shown on a simulated two-armed demonstration.

Every FlexiTac frame is a grid of numbers, one per taxel: 12 rows by 32 columns on a standard sensor. Before a policy can learn from it, you choose how to represent it. There are two ways, and the difference is whether touch knows *where* it happens.

|  | 2D tactile map | 3D tactile points |
|---|---|---|
| **The policy gets** | One 12 × 32 map per pad | Every taxel as a 3D point with its reading, in one point cloud with the camera's points |
| **You need** | Only the sensor | Where each pad sits on the robot, its joint positions and a depth camera |
| **Encoder** | An MLP or a small CNN | A point-cloud network such as PointNet |
| **Used by** | [LeFlexiTac](https://tna001-ai.github.io/LeFlexiTac/), [Touch in the Wild](https://binghao-huang.github.io/touch_in_the_wild/) | [3D-ViTac](https://binghao-huang.github.io/3D-ViTac/), [VT-Refine](https://binghao-huang.github.io/vt_refine/) |

## 2D: a map per pad

The firmware sends each frame as `uint8[12][32]`, row by row ([PyFlexiTac](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/pyflexitac/#python)). Subtract each taxel's resting baseline and scale, and every reading lies between 0 and 1. Keep the numbers on their grid, colour them by value, and the array is an image:

![A 12 by 32 grid of readings, mostly 0; the pressed taxels form a slanted band at one end of the pad](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/tactile-map.svg)

*One pad at one moment: 384 readings on its 12 × 32 grid (row, column). The pressed taxels form a band where the plug lies across the pad. From the simulated demonstration below (right arm, left finger), at the same moment as its 3D view; the simulator reports force divided by 10 N.*

A policy can take the map in two ways:

- **As a vector.** Flatten the 384 readings into one list and feed it to an MLP. It's the simplest input, but the network has to learn which taxels are neighbours.
- **As an image.** Keep the grid and use a small CNN, as for a one-channel camera image, so a contact's shape looks the same wherever it falls on the pad. LeFlexiTac does this: three 3 × 3 convolution layers with pooling turn each map into 256 features, which become extra tokens for ACT, or part of Diffusion Policy's conditioning ([encoder](https://github.com/TNA001-AI/lerobot_tactile/blob/6e59779ac4a711155474477e7ab6997d7160ead0/src/lerobot/policies/tactile/encoder.py)). Touch in the Wild treats touch as images too: its pre-training learns to rebuild masked tactile images from the camera image.

Settle two things before you record:

- **How you normalize.** PyFlexiTac's `normalized` divides each frame by its own peak once there is contact, so it keeps the shape of a contact but not how hard it is ([details](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/pyflexitac/#python)). LeFlexiTac records these maps, and VT-Refine uses the same kind of rule: each pad is scaled by its own peak once it is pressed. If force matters, record `raw` and the baseline too. Either way, normalize the same way in training and on the robot.
- **Which pad is which.** Keep the pads in a fixed order and orientation. Touch in the Wild stores its two pads side by side, as one 12 × 64 map per frame.

**What a map can't tell the policy is where the pad is.** The same line of contact means something different when the gripper is turned or the object is higher, and the policy has to work that out from the joint angles. 3D tactile points put it in the data.

## 3D: tactile points

[3D-ViTac](https://binghao-huang.github.io/3D-ViTac/) (CoRL 2024) puts every taxel in the same 3D frame as the camera's points, so fingers, contacts and objects share one point cloud. [VT-Refine](https://binghao-huang.github.io/vt_refine/) (CoRL 2025) does the same on the two-armed ALOHA robot. The viewer shows one plug–socket demonstration from [FlexiTac's Isaac Sim simulation](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/simulation/#isaac-sim), with a pad on each of ALOHA's four fingers.

![One frame of a simulated plug–socket insertion: the camera picture in a corner, grey camera points of the grippers, plug and socket, and four pads of tactile points with the pressed taxels in orange](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/isaac-frame.webp)

The right arm holds the plug over the socket in the left hand. **Inset:** the camera's picture. **Grey:** the points the same camera sees, 1,024 of them here so they read clearly (VT-Refine keeps 512). **Purple to yellow:** the four pads' 1,536 tactile points, colored by reading on the viridis scale (purple where nothing presses). On the right, the same readings as 2D maps; below, the joint positions the policy also gets. Drag to turn it, **Camera view** goes back to the camera, and play runs the demonstration at its recorded 30 frames a second.

### How a frame is built

1. **Proprioception**
   Read the 16 joint positions of both arms and grippers: per arm, 6 joints and 2 fingers. They do two jobs. Forward kinematics turns them into each pad's pose, which the next step needs, and they go to the policy as an input of their own, through a small MLP. (That is the design in both papers. VT-Refine's released ALOHA config leaves this input out and uses the cloud alone.)
2. **Tactile points**
   Each taxel has a fixed spot on its pad: a 12 × 32 grid, 2 mm apart. Moving the grid by its pad's pose puts every taxel in the table's frame (its origin is the centre of the table). Each tactile point carries its reading. Untouched taxels stay, with a reading of 0, so there are always 4 × 384 = 1,536 of them, and they also show where the fingers are.
3. **Camera points**
   The depth camera's image becomes 3D points in the same table frame. Points outside a box around the workspace are dropped, and 512 of the rest are kept. They carry no colour.
4. **One point cloud**
   Both sets go into one cloud of 2,048 points. Each point has five numbers: x, y, z, the reading (0 for camera points), and a flag that tells the two kinds apart (0 for the camera, 1 for touch).
5. **Encoder and policy**
   A PointNet runs the same small network on every point, then keeps the maximum of each feature over all points, so the order of the points doesn't matter. With the joint features, the result conditions a Diffusion Policy. In VT-Refine it sees the last two frames, predicts the next 16 steps of target joint positions, runs 8 of them, then looks again. 3D-ViTac uses PointNet++.

### In simulation

VT-Refine builds the same observation in simulation, so a policy trained on real demonstrations can keep training there with reinforcement learning. The taxel grid is laid on each simulated pad, the physics engine gives the pad's pose, and each reading comes from how far the taxel presses into the object, normalized with the same rule as the real pads. Noise is added to the simulated camera points only. See [Tactile simulation](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/simulation/#vt-refine).

The viewer above comes from FlexiTac's Isaac Sim simulation in the same way. Its tactile sensors give each taxel's position and reading directly. The picture and the camera points come from the simulated camera's color and depth images, so the cloud has no sensor noise, and the table is cropped away just above its surface, as on a real robot ([recording script](https://github.com/FlexiTac/FlexiTac.github.io/blob/main/doc/_src/tools/isaac_sample.py)).

## The data

VT-Refine's pre-training data, its real-robot demonstrations, stores every step as plain arrays. For the ALOHA tasks:

| Array | Shape per step | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| `point_cloud` | 3 × 512 | Camera points: x, y, z in metres, in the table's frame |
| `tactile_points` | 4 × 1,536 | The four pads' 384 taxels each: x, y, z and the reading (0 to 1, each pad scaled by its own peak) |
| `joint_states` | 16 | Joint positions: per arm, 6 joints and 2 fingers, left arm first, scaled to −1…1 |
| `actions` | 16 | Target joint positions, in the same order and scale |
| `traj_lengths` | one per demonstration | Its number of steps, to split the arrays into demonstrations |

The pads are in the order left arm left finger, left arm right finger, right arm left finger, right arm right finger. `normalization.pth`, next to each `train.npz`, holds the ranges to turn joint values and actions back into radians and metres.

To get the 2D maps back from this data, or to build the five-channel cloud yourself:

```python
import numpy as np

d = np.load("train.npz")                    # plain arrays; no pickle needed
pc, tac = d["point_cloud"][t], d["tactile_points"][t]   # (3, 512), (4, 1536)

# 2D: each pad's 384 points are stored column by column
maps = tac[3].reshape(4, 32, 12).transpose(0, 2, 1)       # (4, 12, 32)

# 3D: x, y, z, reading, flag
cloud = np.concatenate([
    np.vstack([pc,  np.zeros((2, 512))]),    # camera points: reading 0, flag 0
    np.vstack([tac, np.ones((1, 1536))]),    # tactile points: reading, flag 1
], axis=1)                                   # (5, 2048)
```

The data is about 909 MB, under CC BY-NC 4.0. Download it with `data/fetch_vt-refine_data.sh` from the [VT-Refine repository](https://github.com/NVlabs/vt-refine).


---

# Imitation learning with touch (in progress)

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/imitation-learning/

> ACT and Diffusion Policy.

> **Coming soon**
>
> We're writing a full guide to this topic. Until then, both [data-collection setups](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/data-collection/) come with training code you can use today.

## Available today

### LeFlexiTac: ACT and Diffusion Policy

LeFlexiTac trains policies on the LeRobot datasets you [record with it](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/data-collection/#teleoperation). Touch is an extra input, switched on with `--policy.use_tactile=true`. On tube insertion, peg-in-hole and pen retrieval from a bag, the tactile policies beat their vision-only versions in every reported comparison ([results](https://tna001-ai.github.io/LeFlexiTac/)).

Train with and without touch (`--policy.use_tactile=true` / `false`) on a Linux machine with a CUDA GPU, then roll the checkpoint out on the arm. Train and run a policy at the same frame rate you recorded at. Steps 09–10 of the [LeFlexiTac docs](https://tna001-ai.github.io/LeFlexiTac/docs.html#reproduction) have the training and evaluation commands, and the same page ends with practical tips on calibration, camera placement and frame rates.

### Touch in the Wild: Diffusion Policy

Touch in the Wild trains a Diffusion Policy conditioned on its [pretrained visuo-tactile encoder](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/pretraining/#touch-in-the-wild), then runs it on a uFactory xArm 850 with the same fingers and sensors.

**To run policies you need:** a uFactory xArm 850 with the xArm Gripper, the printed finger holder and GoPro mount from the [gripper guide](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Gxd2PzVo-sH_XbvnVw_r3eI5i3I3t0rr7JdhpN1PJMA/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.dcjpnwh7wh40), an HDMI capture card for the GoPro feed, and an NVIDIA GPU for training. [README: Training](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild#training-diffusionpolicies) · [Real-world deployment](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild#realworld-deployment)

# Tactile simulation

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/simulation/

> Simulate FlexiTac pads in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, then replay tactile trajectories and record visuo-tactile demonstrations in the browser. Plus VT-Refine, the sim fine-tuning research behind it.

The simulation lets you work with touch without any hardware. Simulated pads give the same 12 × 32 taxel grid as a FlexiTac-V2 sensor, on the fingers of a robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The current release is the **FlexiTac tactile simulation in Isaac Sim**, which this page shows you how to build and run. It uses the same bimanual plug–socket setup and the same pad layout as **VT-Refine**, the research on fine-tuning visuo-tactile policies in simulation, whose own code runs on the older Isaac Gym.

|  | Isaac Sim simulation (current release) | VT-Refine (research code) |
|---|---|---|
| **Simulator** | Isaac Sim 6.2 with Isaac Lab 3.0 | Isaac Gym Preview (TacSL build), in Docker |
| **Robot and task** | Bimanual ALOHA robot, plug–socket insertion | ALOHA-style tabletop arms and a two-arm Kinova robot, plug–socket insertion |
| **Simulated pads** | 12 × 32 taxels at 2 mm on all four fingers | 12 × 32 at 2 mm on the ALOHA setup |
| **What you do with it** | Replay trajectories with live tactile heatmaps; teleoperate in the browser and record demonstrations | Pre-train a visuo-tactile policy, then fine-tune it with reinforcement learning |
| **Code** | [FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation](https://github.com/binghao-huang/FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation) | [NVlabs/vt-refine](https://github.com/NVlabs/vt-refine) |

## Build the Isaac Sim simulation

The repository is an Isaac Lab tree with two additions: a tactile sensor for FlexiTac pads, and an ALOHA environment whose four fingers each carry a simulated pad.

**You need:** a Linux x86_64 computer (Ubuntu 22.04 or newer) with an NVIDIA RTX GPU and a driver of version 580.65 or newer, plus git and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). Isaac Sim, PyTorch and Isaac Lab take about 30 GB. The trajectory viewer opens a desktop window; the browser interface can run headless. No FlexiTac hardware is needed.

1. **Clone the repository**
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/binghao-huang/FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation.git
   cd FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation
   ```
2. **Create a Python 3.12 environment**
   *FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation/*
   ```bash
   uv venv --python 3.12 --seed env_isaaclab
   source env_isaaclab/bin/activate
   ```
3. **Install Isaac Sim 6.2 and PyTorch**
   The CUDA 13 build of PyTorch is the one Isaac Lab 3.0 pins:
   *FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation/*
   ```bash
   uv pip install "isaacsim[all,extscache]==6.2.0" --extra-index-url https://pypi.nvidia.com --index-strategy unsafe-best-match
   uv pip install -U torch==2.11.0 torchvision==0.26.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130
   ```
   The first launch asks you to accept the NVIDIA Omniverse EULA; `export OMNI_KIT_ACCEPT_EULA=YES` accepts it ahead of time.
4. **Install Isaac Lab and the viewer dependencies**
   `core` installs Isaac Lab's packages, including the FlexiTac sensor, and `visualizer[kit]` the Isaac Sim window:
   *FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation/*
   ```bash
   sudo apt install cmake build-essential
   ./isaaclab.sh -i core
   ./isaaclab.sh -i 'visualizer[kit]'
   uv pip install viser opencv-python
   ```

These steps follow the repository's [installation guide](https://github.com/binghao-huang/FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation#%EF%B8%8F-installation) as of November 2026. If the two differ, the README is the source of truth. For Isaac Sim 5.1 and Isaac Lab 2.3, use the repository's [`isaacsim-5.1` branch](https://github.com/binghao-huang/FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation/tree/isaacsim-5.1) and its README.

## Replay a trajectory with touch

Replay an episode from the bundled sample dataset. The ALOHA robot repeats the recorded motion, and a separate window shows the four finger pads as live tactile heatmaps.

*FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation/*

```bash
./isaaclab.sh -p Isaacsim_tactile_env/reply_with_tactile.py \
    --dataset_npz Isaacsim_tactile_env/data/dataset_train.npz \
    --normalization_pth Isaacsim_tactile_env/data/dataset_normalizer.npz \
    --episode_idx 3 \
    --replay_key joint_states \
    --steps_per_frame 3
```

The script really is named `reply_with_tactile.py`. Change `--episode_idx` to replay another episode, and add `--headless` to run without the Isaac Sim window.

## Teleoperate and record in the browser

Start the web interface, then open **http://localhost:8080**:

*FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation/*

```bash
./isaaclab.sh -p Isaacsim_tactile_env/viser_interface.py \
    --headless \
    --enable_cameras
```

Drag the handle on each end effector to move the two arms, and open or close each gripper with its buttons. The page shows the four tactile heatmaps, the simulated camera and the robot state as you work. **Reset** puts the plug and socket back at the start with a slightly randomized wrist orientation.

**Start Recording** and **Stop Recording** save each demonstration as one `.npz` file in `Isaacsim_tactile_env/output/trajectories/`. Each file holds:

| Key | Shape | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `tactile` | (T, 4, 12, 32) | The four pads, in the order left arm left finger, left arm right finger, right arm left finger, right arm right finger |
| `joint_pos`, `joint_vel` | (T, 16) | Joint positions and velocities of both arms |
| `actions` | (T, 16) | Per arm: target position (3), quaternion (4), gripper (1) |
| `plug_pose`, `socket_pose` | (T, 7) | Object position and wxyz quaternion |
| `rgb` | (T, 480, 640, 3) | Camera images |

## How the simulated pad works

Each finger has a pad with a 12 × 32 grid of taxels at 2 mm pitch, the same layout as a FlexiTac-V2 sensor. On every step, [NVIDIA Warp](https://github.com/NVIDIA/warp) measures how far each taxel has pushed into the object's mesh. That depth becomes a spring force, `clamp(stiffness × depth, 0, max_force)`, which is then divided by `max_force` so each reading lies between 0 and 1. The taxels sit 1.4 mm in front of the pad's face, so a reading starts just before the object touches it; lower `normal_offset` (or pass `--normal_offset` to either script) for smaller contact patches. The grid size, spacing, `normal_offset` (0.0029 m from the pad's mid-plane), `stiffness` (5000) and `max_force` (10) are settings in [`AlohaTactileEnvCfg`](https://github.com/binghao-huang/FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation/blob/3d8006656dcd916f0af4c653f0aa5fba6f3ace6e/Isaacsim_tactile_env/aloha_tactile_cfg.py#L53-L64).

> **What it does not model yet**
>
> - The pads on the left arm sense only the socket, and the pads on the right arm only the plug. Touching anything else, such as the table, gives no signal.
> - Readings are normalized from 0 to 1, not calibrated to a real sensor's output.
> - The environment is built around the ALOHA robot. Using another gripper or pad layout means changing the code; there is no guide for that yet.

## VT-Refine

[VT-Refine](https://binghao-huang.github.io/vt_refine/) (CoRL 2025) trains bimanual assembly policies in three stages, from real to sim and back to real. It first trains a diffusion policy on about 30 real demonstrations per task. Each demonstration records FlexiTac pads on all four fingers together with a camera point cloud, the representation from [3D-ViTac](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/tactile-representation/#3d). Next it fine-tunes that policy in a simulated copy of the setup with large-scale, GPU-parallel reinforcement learning. Finally it moves the policy back to the real robot. The tasks are plug–socket insertions done in mid-air.

The repository has the simulation and training side: a Docker environment, the simulated environments with their tactile model, training configs, and a script that downloads about 909 MB of pre-training data. It does not include trained checkpoints or code for collecting data or running on a real robot.

1. **Install with Docker**
   Clone with submodules and build the image, which installs the TacSL build of Isaac Gym. [README: Installation](https://github.com/NVlabs/vt-refine#installation)
2. **Pre-train the visuo-tactile policy**
   Download the data and train the diffusion policy. [README: Pre-training](https://github.com/NVlabs/vt-refine#pre-training)
3. **Fine-tune in simulation**
   Evaluate the pre-trained policy in simulation, then fine-tune it with reinforcement learning. [README: Evaluation](https://github.com/NVlabs/vt-refine#evaluation---pre-training) · [Fine-tuning](https://github.com/NVlabs/vt-refine#fine-tuning)

> **License and simulator**
>
> The VT-Refine repository is under the NVIDIA License (non-commercial research and evaluation only), and its pre-training data under CC BY-NC 4.0. The submodules it pulls in, with the simulated environments, the tactile model and the training code, are MIT-licensed. It runs on Isaac Gym, which NVIDIA no longer develops. For new work, start from the [Isaac Sim simulation](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/simulation/#isaac-sim) above.


---

## Design files

The V2 files, as linked from the Fabrication Guide. [Order parts](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/order-parts/) explains which to order and how.

| File | Contents |
|---|---|

| [Bottom FPC](https://flexitac.github.io/flexitac-gen/static/vendor/flexitac-v2/Gerber_Bottom_FPC_2026-03-02.zip) | Gerber, EasyEDA Pro export of 2026-03-02 |
| [Reading board 32 × 16](https://flexitac.github.io/flexitac-gen/static/vendor/flexitac-reader/FlexiTac_reading_board_32x16.zip) | Gerber, BOM and pick-and-place ([schematic](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1KEzet6f4s1i1d-GOSpwD5-4Peu2S67hL/view?usp=drive_link)) |
| [Reading board 32 × 32](https://flexitac.github.io/flexitac-gen/static/vendor/flexitac-reader/FlexiTac_reading_board_32x32.zip) | Gerber, BOM and pick-and-place ([schematic](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bmmO034ZeR81Ba8OML_0MlkXvKADsflr/view?usp=drive_link)) |

The parts to buy (Velostat, laminating sheets, polyimide tape, cables, Arduino Nano), with links, are in the [bill of materials](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/order-parts/#bom).
